Six months after Edele died, Lyhne's cousin Mrs. Refstrup lost her husband. He had been a potter, but his business had never prospered, and his long illness had left it badly neglected. His widow stood close to destitution. Supporting seven children was beyond her means. The youngest two stayed with her, along with the eldest, who could work in the factory; the family took in the rest. The Lyhnes received the second boy, fourteen-year-old Erik. He had attended the Latin school in the nearest town without paying tuition. Now he would study under Mr. Bigum alongside Niels and the pastor's son, Frithjof Petersen.

Erik bitterly disliked being held to his books: he wanted to become a sculptor. His father had dismissed that as nonsense, but Lyhne did not object and believed the boy had talent. Nevertheless, a bachelor's degree would give him something to fall back on, Lyhne thought. Besides, a sculptor needed a classical education, or would at least benefit greatly from one. For the present, that settled it. Erik had to content himself with Lönborggaard's fairly extensive collection of fine engravings and elegant bronzes. To a boy who knew only the rubbish left to the local library by a bone-carver with more eccentricity than taste, this meant a great deal. Soon his pencil and modelling-stick were busy. His favourite was Guido Reni, whose fame then surpassed Raphael's and that of the greatest masters. Nothing opens young eyes to artistic beauty more readily than knowing their admiration has the highest authority behind it. Andrea del Sarto, Parmigianino, and Luini, who would matter so much once Erik and his talent found each other, left him cold. Tintoretto's daring and the bitterness of Salvator Rosa and Caravaggio delighted him instead. The very young have no taste for sweetness in art. Even the most delicate miniature painter begins by following Buonarotti; even the gentlest lyric poet launches his first voyage beneath bloody tragedy's black sail.

For Erik, though, art remained a game, only slightly better than his other games. A well-shaped head or skilfully carved horse made him no prouder than striking the church-steeple weather vane with a stone, or swimming to Sönderhagen and back without a pause. Physical contests were his province: strength, stamina, a steady hand, and a trained eye. The games Niels and Frithjof preferred meant nothing to him, with imagination directing everything and events and victories existing only in fancy. Soon the others abandoned their old pursuits and followed his lead. The romantic books went unopened. Their endless tale met a rather violent end at a secret meeting in the hayloft, and silence settled over its freshly dug grave. They were even afraid to mention it to Erik. Within days of his arrival they had guessed he would ridicule both the tale and themselves, shame them, and diminish them in their own eyes. His power lay in his own complete freedom from daydreams, fantasies, and enthusiasms. His clear boyish common sense, relentlessly healthy, despised mental peculiarities as children ordinarily despise bodily defects. This frightened Niels and Frithjof. They remade themselves in his image, denying much and hiding more. Niels was especially eager to crush anything within himself that did not belong in Erik's world. With a convert's fierce zeal he mocked Frithjof, whose slower, more loyal nature could not immediately exchange the old for the new. Beneath that cruel teasing lay jealousy. Niels had loved Erik from the first day, while Erik, shyly detached, half unwilling and half superior, barely and grudgingly consented to be loved.

Of all life's emotional bonds, is any more delicate, more sensitive, more ardent than one boy's exquisitely shy love for another? Such love stays silent, never daring a caress or even a revealing glance. It sees clearly, grieves deeply over each fault in the beloved, and is composed of longing, admiration, and self-forgetfulness, of humility and pride and quietly breathing happiness.

Erik remained at Lönborggaard little more than a year. During a visit to Copenhagen, Lyhne mentioned him to a leading sculptor and showed some of his sketches. The sculptor, Mikkelsen, pronounced this genuine talent and further academic study a waste of time. Giving a nude figure a Greek name required little classical learning. They therefore decided to send Erik straight to the city, where he would attend the Academy and work in Mikkelsen's studio.

On his final afternoon, Erik and Niels sat in their room. Niels looked through pictures in a penny magazine; Erik was immersed in Spengler's critical catalogue of the Christiansborg art collection. How many times he had leafed through it, trying to imagine the paintings from its naïve descriptions! Sometimes longing made him almost ill: he wanted to see all that art and beauty for himself, grasp it as something real, and possess its splendour of colour and line by the sheer force of his enthusiasm. Yet how often he had shut the book in exhaustion, tired of staring into that drifting, fantastic mist of language which would not take substance or shape, would yield nothing, but kept shifting indistinctly—flowing and slipping away, flowing and slipping away.

Today everything had changed. He knew that the figures described in the book would soon cease to be dreamland shadows, and its promises made him feel rich. The pictures appeared to him as never before, flaring like bright, many-coloured suns from a golden mist that danced with gold.
He asked Niels, “What picture are you looking at?”
Niels indicated a portrait in his magazine: Lassen, the hero of the Second of April.
Erik remarked, “What an ugly face!”
“Ugly! But he's a hero. Would you say _this_ man's ugly as well?” Niels turned back to a portrait of a great poet.
“Terribly ugly!” Erik declared, pulling a face. “Look at that nose! And his mouth and eyes, and those clumps of hair round his head!”
Now Niels too could see the ugliness, and had nothing to say. Until then he had never considered that greatness might exist without a beautiful outward form.
Closing Spengler, Erik said, “Before I forget, I ought to give you the deck-house key.”
Gloomily Niels tried to wave the matter away. Erik nevertheless put a small padlock key, suspended from a wide ribbon, around his friend's neck. “Shall we go down?” he asked.

They set off. Beside the garden fence they found Frithjof lying down and eating green gooseberries, his eyes wet at the prospect of the farewell. He was hurt, too, because nobody had come to fetch him. Usually he needed no invitation, but this particular day seemed to call for some ceremony. Wordlessly he offered a handful of berries. The others, having eaten their favourite dishes at dinner, merely turned up their noses.
Erik gave a shudder. “They're sour!”

“That rubbish will give you indigestion!” Niels added, looking scornfully at the offered fruit. “How can you eat it? Throw it away and come to the deck-house.” His hands were in his pockets, so he indicated the key with his chin.
With that, the three boys went on together.

The deck-house was an old ship's cabin, painted green and bought years before at a beach auction. Set up beside the fjord, it had stored tools during construction of the dam, but now stood unused. The boys had claimed it for their ships, bows, arrows, jumping-poles, and other treasures. Especially precious were the forbidden necessities hidden there: gunpowder, tobacco, and matches.
With sombre ceremony Niels unlocked the deck-house. Inside, they felt about in the dark corners of the empty bunks until they located their belongings.
His head buried in a far corner, Erik announced, “I've decided I'm going to blow up my ship.”
“And mine, and Frithjof's!” Niels cried, making a grand gesture of dedication.
Frithjof protested, “Not mine, by Joe! What'll we have to sail once Erik's gone?”
“What indeed!” Niels echoed mockingly, turning his back in contempt.
Frithjof felt uneasy, but once the others were outside, he carefully shifted his boat into a safer hiding place.

Outside, they quickly packed the powder into the ships in nests of tarred oakum, raised the sails, fitted and lit the fuses, then jumped clear. Running beside them along the shore, they signalled to the imaginary crews. Each accidental change of course was loudly explained as proof of the captain's seamanship. But both vessels grounded at the point without exploding. Frithjof thus had the chance to offer up his cap's wadding nobly, so that new and better fuses could be made.

Under full sail the ships headed towards Sjaelland reef. Around them the Britisher's massive frigates lurched into a closed ring, white foam flying about their black bows, the forward guns filling the air with harsh thunder. Closer and closer came the _Albion_ and the _Conqueror_, their towering figure-heads brilliant in red and blue and glittering gold. Grey masses of canvas concealed the horizon. Huge white smoke-clouds rolled out and drifted low like a veil across the sunlit sparkle of the waves. Then a feeble little puff split the deck of Erik's ship. The oakum ignited; red fire burst out. Quick flames licked up the shrouds, ran along the spars, smouldered through the bolt-rope, and leapt like long lightning-streaks into the sails. Burning canvas shrank, tore, and flew seaward in large black flakes. High on the narrow summit of the schooner-mast the Danebrog still waved. Its staff burnt through, and the flag flapped like red wings impatient for battle. Then fire seized it too. Black with smoke, rudderless and without a helmsman, the dead, helpless ship drifted at the mercy of wind and breakers. Niels's ship burned less successfully. Its powder caught, some smoke appeared, and nothing more. That was not enough.
From the point Niels shouted, “Hey, there! Send her down! Turn the starboard cannon towards the aft hatch and fire a volley!” He stooped for a stone. “Ready, fire!” It flew from his hand.

Erik and Frithjof did the same, and soon the hull lay in pieces. They destroyed Erik's ship as well. Dragging the wreckage ashore, they heaped it with dry grass and seaweed to make a bonfire. Thick smoke rose from the burning pile, while crystals clinging to the weed popped and crackled in the fierce heat.

For a long while they sat silently around the fire. Then Niels, still sunk in gloom, suddenly stood and fetched everything he owned from the deck-house. He broke it all into fragments and fed it to the flames. Erik brought his possessions next; Frithjof contributed some of his too. The sacrificial blaze grew so tall that Erik feared it would be visible from the pasture and started smothering it with wet seaweed. Niels stood motionless, watching the smoke drift down the beach with sorrowful eyes. In the background Frithjof hummed a heroic song. Now and then, secretly, he accompanied it with a bard's sweeping gesture, as if stroking the strings of an unseen harp.

At last the fire dwindled. Erik and Frithjof turned homewards, leaving Niels to lock the deck-house. Afterwards he glanced cautiously at the departing boys, then flung key and ribbon far into the fjord. Erik happened to look back just then and saw them fall. Quickly he turned away again and challenged Frithjof to a race.
On the following day Erik departed.
For a time they missed him acutely and bitterly. Their lives had gradually come to depend on being shared by three. Three meant company, variety, change. Two meant boredom and no life at all.
What could two possibly find to occupy themselves with?
Could just two shoot at a target, or play ball? Friday and Robinson Crusoe were possible, certainly—but then who would play the savages?

Those Sundays! Niels grew so tired of living that he first revised his geography, then used Mr. Bigum's large atlas to push far beyond the required lessons. Eventually he began reading the entire Bible and keeping a diary. Frithjof, meanwhile, sank so low in his absolute loneliness that he sought comfort by playing with his sisters.

In time their memories lost some brightness and their longing its sharpest edge. On a quiet evening, the sun reddening the wall of the solitary room, the distant cuckoo's monotonous call might fade and leave the stillness wider and deeper. Then longing would steal into Niels and drain his strength. But it no longer tormented him. It lay vaguely and lightly upon him, half sweet, like pain already passing away.

His letters changed in the same way. At first they loosely strung together questions, wishes, and expressions of regret. Soon they lengthened, turned more towards outward events, and told stories. A polished style ran through them, hiding between the lines a conscious satisfaction in writing so well.

As the weeks went by, things that had not dared appear while Erik was there began raising their heads. Imagination scattered vivid flowers across the dull peace of an uneventful existence. Dreams wrapped Niels's mind in their atmosphere, carrying life's enticing fragrance. Concealed within that fragrance was the subtle poison of fantasies thirsty for life.

So Niels grows, while every influence of childhood works upon the yielding clay. Everything leaves a shape, everything matters: what happened and what was dreamed, what is known and what is only foreshadowed. Each lays a gentle but certain touch on that pattern of lines destined first to be carved deeper, then flattened and smoothed away.
